screens.title: Containers vs Serverless — Where risks differ
screens.narratorSegment: Start by mapping architecture to risk. Containers package an application and its dependencies into a lightweight unit that shares the host kernel. This sharing means a container breakout or excessive capabilities can damage the host or neighbor containers. Serverless shifts responsibility for infrastructure to the cloud provider, but it concentrates risk in configuration and code: overly broad IAM roles, unvalidated inputs, or mismanaged secrets grant attackers wide access even without VM-level privileges. A concrete example: a container running as root with unnecessary tools can be used to pivot to the node if a vulnerability is exploited, while an AWS Lambda function with an overly permissive role could access unrelated S3 buckets if compromised. A common misconception is that serverless removes all security work — in reality, it moves it from patch management to policy, identity, and input validation. Key practices follow directly from this contrast: reduce image surface area and kernel-facing privileges for containers; for serverless, design narrow IAM roles, use resource-based policies, and validate every event or HTTP payload. Reflect on which parts of your stack are infrastructure-managed and which are your responsibility, because that determines where to apply controls.

keyIdea.text: Containers expose host-facing risk through kernel sharing; serverless exposes identity and configuration risks through IAM and function inputs.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Containers vs Serverless
Core Concept
Container Risk Profile
Shared kernel, image supply chain, runtime capabilities
  • • Attackers may exploit vulnerable packages inside images or escalate via container capabilities.
  • • Running as root or leaving build tools increases host compromise risk.
  • • Image provenance matters — unsigned or unscanned images may contain known CVEs.
Concrete Example
A container built from a large OS image includes compilers and package managers. If the app is exploited, the attacker can download tools and attempt node escape. Removing these tools and running as non-root blocks this path.
Serverless Risk Profile
Provider-managed runtime, identity-focused, configuration-sensitive
  • • A compromised function inherits the permissions of its IAM role, so over-permissioned roles enlarge blast radius.
  • • Input validation failures can lead to injection or unauthorized operations on backend resources.
  • Use of secrets in environment variables or code can leak sensitive credentials if not managed externally.
Concrete Example
A function with broad S3 permissions can be used to exfiltrate data from unrelated buckets. Narrowing the role to specific bucket paths and actions prevents this attack vector.
Key Takeaway

Match controls to architecture: host-facing controls for containers, identity and config controls for serverless.

Common Mistake

Assuming serverless eliminates security work; it instead moves it to identity and input handling.

Pro Tip

Inventory what you manage versus what the provider manages to prioritize controls effectively.

screens.title: Dockerfile Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A secure container image starts with how you write the Dockerfile. Key rules are straightforward but easy to miss: pick a minimal base image to reduce installed packages, avoid the unstable or unpredictable 'latest' tag, and use multi-stage builds to keep build-time dependencies out of the final runtime image. Always create and switch to a non-root user so the process inside the container cannot act with root privileges. Remove compilers and package managers from the final image and use image scanning tools in CI to detect known vulnerabilities. Signing images complements scanning by ensuring integrity and supply-chain provenance. A concrete example: a multi-stage Python build installs dependencies only in the builder stage and copies compiled artifacts into a slim final image that runs as an unprivileged user. A common misconception is that build-time convenience is safe in production; leaving build tools in images is a persistent source of compromise. The practical outcome of following these practices is twofold: fewer vulnerabilities shipped and smaller blast radius if a container is exploited. Ask yourself: when was the last time your pipeline scanned and signed every image before deploy?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Dockerfile Best Practices
Definition
Guiding rules
  • • Use minimal base images to limit installed packages and CVEs.
  • • Avoid 'latest' tags to prevent unexpected changes at build time.
  • • Use multi-stage builds to strip build dependencies from final images.
  • • Create and switch to a non-root user and remove unnecessary tools.
  • • Scan and sign images in CI before push to registries.
Why it matters
Smaller, cleaner images reduce the number of vulnerabilities and make provenance verification feasible across teams.
Concrete Example
A multi-stage Python build that runs as non-root
# Stage 1: build
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: final
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages
COPY . .
RUN adduser --system --no-create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python3", "app.py"]
Common Mistake
Leaving compilers or package managers in the final image gives attackers tools for lateral movement if exploited.

screens.title: From Vulnerable to Hardened: Dockerfile Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a hands-on hardening of a vulnerable Dockerfile. The vulnerable file uses a full language image, installs dependencies at runtime, and runs as root — convenient for development but dangerous in production. The safe version uses a multi-stage build: compile dependencies in a builder stage, copy only runtime artifacts into a slimmer final stage, and create a dedicated non-root user. This reduces the surface area, removes build tools from the runtime image, and ensures processes cannot act as root. In CI, add image scanning after build and before push so vulnerabilities are flagged early. Also consider signing the final image to assert provenance. A concrete change is replacing a plain FROM python:3.9 with a slim base and copying only installed site-packages. Misconception to avoid: building everything in one layer because it seems faster; in reality it bakes unnecessary tools into the image. After this walkthrough, you should be able to apply the same transformation to other language stacks and add scanning and signing steps into your pipeline. From Vulnerable to Hardened: Dockerfile Walkthrough means convert single-stage builds into multi-stage builds, remove build tools, and run as non-root to reduce attack surface and privilege.. In practical terms, live code demo: convert a simple dockerfile into a hardened, multi-stage build that runs non-root. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Dockerfile Hardening Demo
Code Walkthrough
Vulnerable Dockerfile
# Vulnerable Dockerfile
FROM python:3.9
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
This image runs as root and includes build-time tools. It uses a general base and installs packages into the runtime image.
Hardened Multi-Stage Dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build dependencies
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Final image
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages
COPY . .
RUN adduser --system --no-create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python3", "app.py"]
Key changes: multi-stage build, removal of build artifacts, and creation of a non-root user. Add image scanning and signing in CI after this stage.
Check Your Understanding
Why is copying only site-packages from the builder stage safer than installing in the final image?
Common Mistake
Keeping package managers and compilers in the final image increases tools available to attackers.
Key Takeaway

Multi-stage builds and non-root execution are simple, high-impact hardening steps.

screens.title: Image Scanning and Signing
screens.narratorSegment: Image scanning and signing are complementary safeguards. Scanning tools inspect OS packages and application dependencies to report known CVEs so teams can fail builds or trigger remediation. Signing ensures the image you pull in production is the exact artifact that passed CI checks, limiting supply-chain tampering. In practice, add scanning to the pipeline immediately after build and before registry push, and use signing tools to record an immutable artifact identity. For example, a pipeline stage runs Trivy or Clair to produce a vulnerability report; if high-severity findings appear, the pipeline blocks promotion. Once an image passes, tools like Cosign create a signature that a cluster admission controller or a deployment job can verify. A common misconception is that scanning alone is enough — but without signing, a registry can be modified or a different image could be pulled. Together, scanning and signing provide both detection and trust, and they fit naturally into automated CI/CD gates to keep risky images out of clusters. Image Scanning and Signing means use scanning to detect vulnerabilities and signing to guarantee image integrity before deployment.. In practical terms, automate vulnerability detection and assert image provenance in ci/cd. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Image Scanning & Signing
Definition
Image Scanning
Detect known vulnerabilities before deployment
  • • Integrate Trivy, Clair, or Anchore into CI to fail on high-risk CVEs.
  • • Scan both OS packages and language dependencies to find transitive issues.
  • • Store reports with the build metadata for audits and triage.
Example
Run a scan after building an image; block promotion on high-severity matches and open a ticket for remediation.
Image Signing
Assert integrity and provenance of images
  • • Use signing tools to create verifiable metadata for each promoted image.
  • • Enforce verification in deploy pipelines or admission controllers in clusters.
  • • Treat signatures as part of your SBOM and audit trail.
Common Mistake
Relying on scanning alone without signing allows an attacker to swap images in registries after scans pass.
Key Takeaway

Combine automated scanning with signing and verification to detect vulnerabilities and ensure only trusted images reach runtime.

screens.title: Kubernetes Security Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes adds orchestration capabilities and with them new controls you must configure correctly. Pod Security Standards set admission rules for pods, defining profiles from Privileged to Restricted; using the Restricted profile enforces settings like runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and dropping capabilities. RBAC governs who and what can call the Kubernetes A P I, so service accounts must follow least privilege. Network Policies control pod-to-pod communication; by default, pods can talk freely, so policies are needed to segment services and reduce lateral movement. A practical scenario: enforce a Restricted PSS for user workloads, create narrow RBAC roles for service accounts, and apply Network Policies that allow only required traffic between front-end and back-end pods. A common misconception is that enabling one control is sufficient — in reality, these layers are complementary. Together they limit what a pod can do, who can influence it, and what network paths it can access. The result is defense-in-depth: even if an attacker compromises a pod process, additional constraints limit damage. Kubernetes Security Fundamentals means pod security standards constrain pod behavior, rbac limits api actions, and network policies restrict traffic, forming complementary defenses.. In practical terms, why pod security standards, rbac, and network policies work together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Pod Security Standards constrain pod behavior, RBAC limits API actions, and Network Policies restrict traffic, forming complementary defenses.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Kubernetes Security Fundamentals
Architecture
Pod Security Standards (PSS)
Profiles: Privileged → Baseline → Restricted
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
containers:
- name: app
  securityContext:
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
These settings reduce kernel-facing privileges and restrict what processes inside the pod can do.
RBAC & Network Policies
Control API actions and network segmentation
  • • RBAC: grant least privilege to service accounts and avoid cluster-admin roles unless required.
  • • NetworkPolicy: deny by default and allow only specific ingress/egress between pods.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress: []
Real-world connection
Enforce these controls via admission controllers and automation to keep clusters consistent.
Common Mistake
Relying only on RBAC without network segmentation still allows lateral movement between pods.
Key Takeaway

Use PSS, RBAC, and Network Policies together to limit capabilities, access, and network reach.

screens.title: Pod Security Standards (PSS) — Enforce Restricted Profile
screens.narratorSegment: Pod Security Standards provide a consistent framework for admitting pods into a cluster. The Restricted profile is the most secure and includes settings such as runAsNonRoot, dropping all capabilities, disabling privilege escalation, and enforcing a read-only root filesystem. These constraints prevent common privilege escalation techniques and reduce the tools available to an attacker inside a container. Use a pod security admission controller or policy engine to enforce these settings at namespace or cluster level. A concrete example is a Deployment spec with pod-level and container-level securityContext fields that set a UID and drop capabilities. A typical misconception is that setting runAsNonRoot is sufficient; while necessary, it should be paired with readOnlyRootFilesystem and cap drops to be effective. When rolling out PSS, start with Baseline for compatibility testing and then move to Restricted for production workloads. Think of PSS as a guardrail that prevents insecure pod configurations from ever running, which is essential for large teams and automated pipelines. In practical terms, practical pod security settings and a deployment snippet to enforce restrictions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Pod Security Standards provide a consistent framework for admitting pods into a cluster. The Restricted profile is the most secure and includes settings such as runAsNonRoot, dropping all capabilities, disabling privilege escalation, and enforcing a read-only root filesystem. These constraints prevent common privilege escalation techniques and reduce the tools available to an attacker inside a container. Use a pod security admission controller or policy engine to enforce these settings at namespace or cluster level. A concrete example is a Deployment spec with pod-level and container-level securityContext fields that set a UID and drop capabilities. A typical misconception is that setting runAsNonRoot is sufficient; while necessary, it should be paired with readOnlyRootFilesystem and cap drops to be effective. When rolling out PSS, start with Baseline for compatibility testing and then move to Restricted for production workloads. Think of PSS as a guardrail that prevents insecure pod configurations from ever running, which is essential for large teams and automated pipelines. Pod Security Standards (PSS) — Enforce Restricted Profile means restricted profile enforces runasnonroot, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, and read-only filesystem to reduce exploitation paths.. In practical terms, practical pod security settings and a deployment snippet to enforce restrictions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PSS enforcement
keyIdea.text: Restricted profile enforces runAsNonRoot, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, and read-only filesystem to reduce exploitation paths.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Pod Security Standards
Process Flow
Restricted Profile — Key Settings
  • • runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser set to a non-zero UID.
  • • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.
  • • capabilities: drop ALL.
  • • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true.
  • • seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault.
Rollout tip
Start in audit/complain mode, fix violations, then enforce Restricted for production.
Example Deployment Snippet
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-secure-image:latest
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Common Mistake
Setting only runAsNonRoot without dropping capabilities still leaves many privilege paths open.
Analogy
PSS is like seat belts and airbags; each safety feature mitigates a different failure mode.
Key Takeaway

Enforce multiple pod-level constraints to meaningfully reduce privilege escalation risk.

screens.title: RBAC, Service Accounts, and Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: Role-Based Access Control is how Kubernetes ensures only authorized identities perform actions against the A P I. Service accounts represent pod identities, and RBAC roles and role bindings attach permissions to those identities. The guiding principle is least privilege: grant only the A P I verbs and resource scope necessary for a workload. For example, an app that needs to read ConfigMaps should not receive permissions to create or delete Pods or modify cluster-wide resources. A common mistake is giving broad roles like cluster-admin for convenience; a compromised pod with that permission can change cluster state and elevate impact. To put this into practice, inventory each service account, define the narrowest set of verbs required, and bind to a namespaced role where possible. Regularly review and rotate service account credentials, and consider automating policy checks in CI so permissions are reviewed as part of code changes. The result is containment: an attacker who compromises a pod only has limited A P I influence rather than cluster-wide power. RBAC, Service Accounts, and Least Privilege means use rbac and scoped service accounts to contain what a compromised pod can do inside the kubernetes api.. In practical terms, design rbac policies so compromised pods cannot manipulate the cluster. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › RBAC & Service Accounts
Core Concept
Design Principles
  • • Grant the minimum verbs and resource scope required by a workload.
  • • Use namespaced roles rather than cluster roles when possible.
  • • Regularly audit bindings and rotate credentials for service accounts.
Example
A backend service should receive read access to a specific ConfigMap and write access to its own Deployment annotations, not broad pod or node privileges.
Operational Steps
  1. 1. Inventory service accounts and their current permissions.
  2. 2. Define narrowly scoped Roles and RoleBindings per application.
  3. 3. Automate checks into CI to prevent overly broad changes.
Common Mistake
Reusing a single service account with broad permissions across many apps multiplies blast radius when compromised.
Key Takeaway

RBAC and scoped service accounts are essential to prevent a compromised pod from altering cluster state or accessing unrelated resources.

screens.title: Network Policies and Segmentation
screens.narratorSegment: Network Policies control which pods can talk to which endpoints. By default, Kubernetes allows free communication between pods, so applying Network Policies creates explicit allow lists that block unexpected traffic. A common pattern is deny-all-ingress for a namespace, then create specific policies that allow front-end pods to connect to back-end pods on required ports. This segmentation limits lateral movement if an attacker gains code execution in one pod. A practical YAML example denies all ingress and then you add policies that permit traffic only from defined podSelectors. Misconception: Network Policies are a substitute for RBAC — they are complementary. RBAC controls A P I access while Network Policies control runtime traffic. When designing policies, think about service intent: which services legitimately need to speak to others? Start with conservative defaults and incrementally open only necessary paths. Combine network policies with egress controls where possible to prevent exfiltration to the internet from compromised pods. Network Policies and Segmentation means deny-by-default network policies and explicit allow rules reduce lateral movement and data exfiltration risk inside clusters.. In practical terms, use network policies to reduce lateral movement and enforce service boundaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Network Policies
Process Flow
Deny-By-Default Pattern
Start locked, allow only necessary paths
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress: []
Apply specific allow rules for services that must communicate, scoped by podSelector and ports.
Design Considerations
  • • Model traffic flows from the application's perspective: which services must talk?
  • • Use labels to group pods and keep policies maintainable.
  • • Test policies in staging before enforcing in production.
Common Mistake
Assuming network policies are automatically applied — many clusters require a network plugin that supports them.
Key Takeaway

Implement deny-by-default network policies and create narrow allow rules that reflect real service needs to minimize lateral movement.

screens.title: Runtime Security, Logging, and Detection
screens.narratorSegment: Runtime security complements build-time hardening and cluster policies by detecting abnormal behavior while applications run. Tools like Falco watch system calls and process behavior inside containers, issuing alerts when activity deviates from expected patterns. Service mesh or eBPF-based tools such as Cilium can provide network-level enforcement and observability. Centralized logging and metrics — for example, sending application logs and container runtime events to a SIEM or cloud monitor — allow you to correlate alerts, investigate incidents, and trigger automated responses. A concrete practice is to define behavioral rules for Falco that alert on shell execution in application containers or outbound connections to unexpected endpoints. A common misconception is that runtime tools replace hardening; instead, they compensate for gaps and provide detection. Effective runtime security pipeline includes alert tuning to reduce noise, playbooks for triage, and integration with orchestration to quarantine or redeploy suspicious workloads. Your goal is to shorten time-to-detect and time-to-respond when prevention controls fail. Runtime Security, Logging, and Detection means runtime tools like falco and cilium plus centralized logs enable detection of anomalous behavior and automated containment workflows.. In practical terms, use runtime tools and centralized logging to detect suspicious container and function behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Runtime Security
Diagram
Detection Tools
  • • Falco: syscall and process behavior detection inside containers.
  • • Cilium: eBPF networking, visibility, and enforcement.
  • • RASP or host-level agents for deeper runtime signals.
Logging & SIEM
Collect container logs, audit events, and runtime alerts centrally to correlate suspicious activity and support investigations.
Example
Alert when an application container spawns a shell or opens outbound connections to unusual addresses and forward alert context to the incident queue.
Response & Automation
  • • Tune alerts to reduce noise and focus on high-fidelity signals.
  • • Integrate with orchestration to quarantine or redeploy compromised workloads.
  • • Maintain playbooks for triage and remediation steps.
Common Mistake
Treating runtime tools as a replacement for hardening rather than as a complementary detection layer.
Key Takeaway

Combine runtime detection, centralized logs, and automated response to detect and contain incidents quickly.

screens.title: Serverless Security Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless reduces infrastructure burden but concentrates responsibility in configuration and code. The most critical control is IAM: assign each function the narrowest role it needs and prefer resource-based policies to limit resource scope. For example, a function that reads from a single input bucket should receive GetObject permission for that specific path, not wildcard S3 permissions. Input validation is equally essential; every event, header, or payload must be validated and sanitized to prevent injection. Secrets must never be hardcoded — use a secrets manager and fetch secrets at runtime. If functions are exposed through an A P I Gateway, add authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and WAF rules to defend against abuse and injection attacks. A common misconception is that small function size means low risk; in fact, a compromised function with broad IAM can access many resources. Concrete steps: define granular IAM policies per function, validate input schemas strictly, use managed secret stores for credentials, and protect public endpoints with gateway controls. These measures dramatically reduce blast radius and prevent many common serverless failures. Serverless Security Best Practices means apply least-privilege iam, strict input validation, external secrets management, and api gateway protections to safeguard functions.. In practical terms, iam least privilege, input validation, secrets management, and api gateway protections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Serverless Security
Comparison
IAM: Least Privilege
Create fine-grained roles for each function and avoid wildcard permissions. Prefer resource scoping in policies.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket/input/*"
    }
  ]
}
Input Validation & Secrets
  • • Validate every event, query parameter, and payload with a schema.
  • • Store secrets in a secret manager and fetch them at runtime instead of hardcoding.
  • • Monitor logs for unusual invocation patterns and errors that indicate abuse.
API Gateway
Protect public functions with authentication, rate limiting, and a WAF to reduce exposure to automated attacks.
Scenario
A function that processes uploaded files should only be able to read a single bucket path, validate file types, and never store credentials in its environment variables.
Common Mistake
Giving functions broad IAM permissions because it's easier during development.
Key Takeaway

Serverless risk is primarily identity and input-related; lock down IAM, validate inputs, and manage secrets to reduce exposure.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three central ideas in mind as you harden cloud-native systems. First, image hygiene matters: use minimal bases, multi-stage builds, non-root users, and automated scanning and signing to prevent vulnerable artifacts from reaching production. Second, cluster controls are layered: Pod Security Standards constrain runtime behavior, RBAC limits A P I capabilities, and Network Policies restrict network flows; use them together for defense-in-depth. Third, serverless security focuses on identity and inputs: grant each function least-privilege IAM, validate every input, and keep secrets in dedicated stores. These concise concepts map directly to practical actions you can add to CI/CD, admission policies, and runtime monitoring. When you design or review deployments, ask whether each of these defenses is present and automated. That checklist keeps risk within manageable bounds and ensures your cloud-native apps remain resilient under attack.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical mental model for securing both containers and serverless functions. You will learn why containers are not full virtual machines, why the host kernel matters, and how small mistakes in a Dockerfile or IAM policy create large risks. We will walk through concrete hardening steps: minimal base images and multi-stage builds for images, scanning and signing images before deploy, enforcing Pod Security Standards and network segmentation in Kubernetes, and applying least-privilege IAM and input validation in serverless functions. Each concept includes an example you can use in a CI/CD pipeline or cluster admission policy, plus the common mistakes to watch for. By the end, you will be able to explain the primary attack surfaces, select the right controls, and apply a repeatable checklist to reduce blast radius across container and serverless deployments. Think about an app you manage: where would you start hardening? That question will guide the hands-on portion.

These objectives translate the chapter into measurable skills. First, you will identify the unique attack vectors for containers and serverless code — this means understanding how shared kernels, image supply chains, and overly permissive IAM expand an attacker’s options. Second, you will implement secure container builds: selecting minimal base images, using multi-stage builds, removing build tools, running as non-root, and integrating image scanning into CI/CD. Third, you will configure Kubernetes controls like Pod Security Standards, enforce read-only root filesystems and dropped capabilities, and use RBAC to limit what service accounts can do. Fourth, you will apply runtime monitoring strategies such as Falco or Cilium to detect suspicious behavior and feed logs into a SIEM. Each objective pairs a technique with why it matters so you can show a verifier how the control reduces blast radius or improves detection.

These secondary objectives focus on operational practices you will apply immediately. First, you will set up image scanning and signing so every artifact in your pipeline has integrity checks and vulnerability reports. Second, you will design Kubernetes RBAC and service accounts that follow least privilege, limiting what a compromised pod can do inside the cluster. Third, you will secure serverless functions by crafting granular IAM roles, using resource-based policies, and validating all inputs to avoid injection and data exposure. Fourth, you will integrate secrets management for both containers and functions, using dedicated secret stores instead of embedding keys in images or code. Together these objectives turn design principles into repeatable controls you can audit and automate. Learning Objectives — Continued means you will learn to automate image validation, enforce least-privilege access, validate inputs, and manage secrets so security scales with deployments.. In practical terms, additional practical skills and verifications. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by mapping architecture to risk. Containers package an application and its dependencies into a lightweight unit that shares the host kernel. This sharing means a container breakout or excessive capabilities can damage the host or neighbor containers. Serverless shifts responsibility for infrastructure to the cloud provider, but it concentrates risk in configuration and code: overly broad IAM roles, unvalidated inputs, or mismanaged secrets grant attackers wide access even without VM-level privileges. A concrete example: a container running as root with unnecessary tools can be used to pivot to the node if a vulnerability is exploited, while an AWS Lambda function with an overly permissive role could access unrelated S3 buckets if compromised. A common misconception is that serverless removes all security work — in reality, it moves it from patch management to policy, identity, and input validation. Key practices follow directly from this contrast: reduce image surface area and kernel-facing privileges for containers; for serverless, design narrow IAM roles, use resource-based policies, and validate every event or HTTP payload. Reflect on which parts of your stack are infrastructure-managed and which are your responsibility, because that determines where to apply controls.

A secure container image starts with how you write the Dockerfile. Key rules are straightforward but easy to miss: pick a minimal base image to reduce installed packages, avoid the unstable or unpredictable 'latest' tag, and use multi-stage builds to keep build-time dependencies out of the final runtime image. Always create and switch to a non-root user so the process inside the container cannot act with root privileges. Remove compilers and package managers from the final image and use image scanning tools in CI to detect known vulnerabilities. Signing images complements scanning by ensuring integrity and supply-chain provenance. A concrete example: a multi-stage Python build installs dependencies only in the builder stage and copies compiled artifacts into a slim final image that runs as an unprivileged user. A common misconception is that build-time convenience is safe in production; leaving build tools in images is a persistent source of compromise. The practical outcome of following these practices is twofold: fewer vulnerabilities shipped and smaller blast radius if a container is exploited. Ask yourself: when was the last time your pipeline scanned and signed every image before deploy?

Let's walk through a hands-on hardening of a vulnerable Dockerfile. The vulnerable file uses a full language image, installs dependencies at runtime, and runs as root — convenient for development but dangerous in production. The safe version uses a multi-stage build: compile dependencies in a builder stage, copy only runtime artifacts into a slimmer final stage, and create a dedicated non-root user. This reduces the surface area, removes build tools from the runtime image, and ensures processes cannot act as root. In CI, add image scanning after build and before push so vulnerabilities are flagged early. Also consider signing the final image to assert provenance. A concrete change is replacing a plain FROM python:3.9 with a slim base and copying only installed site-packages. Misconception to avoid: building everything in one layer because it seems faster; in reality it bakes unnecessary tools into the image. After this walkthrough, you should be able to apply the same transformation to other language stacks and add scanning and signing steps into your pipeline. From Vulnerable to Hardened: Dockerfile Walkthrough means convert single-stage builds into multi-stage builds, remove build tools, and run as non-root to reduce attack surface and privilege.. In practical terms, live code demo: convert a simple dockerfile into a hardened, multi-stage build that runs non-root. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Image scanning and signing are complementary safeguards. Scanning tools inspect OS packages and application dependencies to report known CVEs so teams can fail builds or trigger remediation. Signing ensures the image you pull in production is the exact artifact that passed CI checks, limiting supply-chain tampering. In practice, add scanning to the pipeline immediately after build and before registry push, and use signing tools to record an immutable artifact identity. For example, a pipeline stage runs Trivy or Clair to produce a vulnerability report; if high-severity findings appear, the pipeline blocks promotion. Once an image passes, tools like Cosign create a signature that a cluster admission controller or a deployment job can verify. A common misconception is that scanning alone is enough — but without signing, a registry can be modified or a different image could be pulled. Together, scanning and signing provide both detection and trust, and they fit naturally into automated CI/CD gates to keep risky images out of clusters. Image Scanning and Signing means use scanning to detect vulnerabilities and signing to guarantee image integrity before deployment.. In practical terms, automate vulnerability detection and assert image provenance in ci/cd. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Role-Based Access Control is how Kubernetes ensures only authorized identities perform actions against the A P I. Service accounts represent pod identities, and RBAC roles and role bindings attach permissions to those identities. The guiding principle is least privilege: grant only the A P I verbs and resource scope necessary for a workload. For example, an app that needs to read ConfigMaps should not receive permissions to create or delete Pods or modify cluster-wide resources. A common mistake is giving broad roles like cluster-admin for convenience; a compromised pod with that permission can change cluster state and elevate impact. To put this into practice, inventory each service account, define the narrowest set of verbs required, and bind to a namespaced role where possible. Regularly review and rotate service account credentials, and consider automating policy checks in CI so permissions are reviewed as part of code changes. Serverless reduces infrastructure burden but concentrates responsibility in configuration and code. The most critical control is IAM: assign each function the narrowest role it needs and prefer resource-based policies to limit resource scope. For example, a function that reads from a single input bucket should receive GetObject permission for that specific path, not wildcard S3 permissions. Input validation is equally essential; every event, header, or payload must be validated and sanitized to prevent injection. Secrets must never be hardcoded — use a secrets manager and fetch secrets at runtime. Keep three central ideas in mind as you harden cloud-native systems. First, image hygiene matters: use minimal bases, multi-stage builds, non-root users, and automated scanning and signing to prevent vulnerable artifacts from reaching production. Second, cluster controls are layered: Pod Security Standards constrain runtime behavior, RBAC limits A P I capabilities, and Network Policies restrict network flows; use them together for defense-in-depth. Third, serverless security focuses on identity and inputs: grant each function least-privilege IAM, validate every input, and keep secrets in dedicated stores. These concise concepts map directly to practical actions you can add to CI/CD, admission policies, and runtime monitoring. When you design or review deployments, ask whether each of these defenses is present and automated. That checklist keeps risk within manageable bounds and ensures your cloud-native apps remain resilient under attack.
